title: Mishpatim: straight after Sinai, the details
hook: after the thunder come laws about workers, damages and loans
tomorrow: Mishpatim: the heart of a stranger (Exodus 23:9)

segments.voice: Yesterday Yitro ended with lo tachmod, do not covet. Your line was the last word is inside. Did you catch one envy before it turned into a plan? Today, a new portion, and a sudden change of tone. Day three hundred forty-eight.

A hospital lobby often has big words on the wall: compassion, dignity, care. The words don't wash anyone's hands. What carries them out is a laminated checklist by the sink, a chart at the foot of the bed, a nurse checking the name on a wristband twice. The big words live in the small print. The Torah works the same way. One portion is full of thunder, lightning, a mountain on fire and the voice of God. The very next portion opens, almost without a pause, with laws about servants, injuries, a goring ox, and an open pit.
screen: `BIG WORDS ON THE LOBBY WALL.` → `A CHECKLIST BY THE SINK.` → `AFTER THE THUNDER, AN OPEN PIT.`

segments.voice: The portion's first verse, in the old Jewish translation: "Now these are the ordinances which thou shalt set before them." Ordinances, in Hebrew, mishpatim: laws, judgments, the rules a court would use. And they're astonishingly practical. A Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year. If you dig a pit and leave it open and an animal falls in, you pay. If your ox has gored before and you didn't keep it in, you're responsible. If you lend money to a poor person, don't charge interest. If you take a neighbor's cloak as a pledge, give it back before sunset, because it's what they sleep in. Rashi, the medieval commentator, stops on the first word of the verse. In Hebrew it's not just these, it's and these. That little and, he says, joins this portion to the one before. Just as the Ten Words came from Sinai, so did these. For Rashi, the goring ox comes from the same place as the thunder. He also notices set before them, and says it means like a table that's set, ready to eat from, with everything laid out clearly. That's the point of the portion. Sinai wasn't meant to stay on the mountain. It was meant to come down into the barn, the field, the loan, the paycheck. Holiness, in this portion, doesn't float. It shows up in the fine print.
screen: `MISHPATIM: THE ORDINANCES.` · `SERVANTS, PITS, OXEN, LOANS.` · `RASHI: AND THESE, ALSO FROM SINAI.` · `SET LIKE A TABLE.` · then, large: `HOLINESS LIVES IN DETAILS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor an ordinary rule. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small rule in your life you usually treat as a nuisance. Returning the shopping cart. Paying someone on time. Cleaning up after yourself at work. Driving at the limit near a school. Picture the person on the other end of that rule: the worker collecting carts, the contractor waiting for payment, the child crossing the street. Let the rule become a way of caring for them. The bell holds the time.
Mishpatim. Ordinances, laws, judgments. The name of the portion that brings Sinai down into workers, damages and loans.
Your line: holiness lives in details. Today, do one small, boring, decent thing properly, as if it came from the mountain. Day three hundred forty-eight.
